code.title: Correlated vs non-correlated subquery plans
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept INT, salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha',1,50),(2,'Ben',1,70),(3,'Cy',2,40),(4,'Di',2,90),(5,'Eli',2,50);
""")
# Non-correlated: inner query is self-contained, evaluated once (overall avg = 60)
q1 = "SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp)"
# Correlated: inner query uses e.dept from the outer row (dept avg)
q2 = """SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE salary >
        (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept)"""
print("rows:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM emp").fetchall())
print("above company avg:", [r[0] for r in db.execute(q1)])
print("above own dept avg:", [r[0] for r in db.execute(q2)])
# The plan text names the difference
for q in (q1, q2):
    plan = [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + q)]
    print([p for p in plan if "SUBQUERY" in p])

followUps:
Yes. A correlated subquery in the SELECT list is allowed as long as it returns exactly one column and at most one row (a scalar subquery); if it returns two rows most engines raise an error.

Example: SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id) FROM customers c. A customer with no orders gets 0 from COUNT, but a SUM or MAX would give NULL. Cost without an index on o.cust_id is O(N x M).

Turn the subquery into a grouped derived table and join it on the correlation key. Use a LEFT JOIN so outer rows without matches survive.

SELECT e.name FROM emp e
JOIN (SELECT dept, AVG(salary) a FROM emp GROUP BY dept) d
  ON d.dept = e.dept
WHERE e.salary > d.a;

This reads emp twice, once to group (O(N)) and once to join, instead of once per outer row. For counts add COALESCE(n, 0).

code.title: NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT);  -- NULL = guest order
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ana'),(2,'Bo'),(3,'Cat');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1),(11,NULL);
""")
queries = {
 "NOT IN (trap)": "SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)",
 "NOT IN + IS NOT NULL": """SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN
      (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL)""",
 "NOT EXISTS": """SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS
      (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)""",
 "LEFT JOIN anti-join": """SELECT c.name FROM customers c
      LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL""",
}
print("orders:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM orders").fetchall())
for label, q in queries.items():
    # NOT IN returns nothing because 'id <> NULL' is UNKNOWN, never TRUE
    print(label, "->", [r[0] for r in db.execute(q)])

followUps:
Yes, but the damage is smaller. x IN (a, b, NULL) can still be TRUE when x equals a or b, so matching rows are returned; the NULL only turns the non-matching rows into UNKNOWN, and WHERE drops those anyway.

So 2 IN (1, 2, NULL) is TRUE, while 3 IN (1, 2, NULL) is UNKNOWN (treated as no match). The result is the same as ignoring the NULL, which is why IN looks safe and only the negation breaks.

Because NOT IN must keep track of NULLs, the planner often cannot turn it into an anti-join and falls back to a hashed or per-row subplan.

NOT EXISTS has simple two-valued logic, so PostgreSQL plans a hash anti-join: O(N + M). A NOT IN over a large subquery that may contain NULL can spill the hashed subplan to disk or rescan it for each outer row, which is O(N x M). Same rows when the column is NOT NULL, very different plans otherwise.

code.title: IN, EXISTS and JOIN give the same rows

followUps:
SQLite builds the subquery result once into a temporary list (shown as LIST SUBQUERY in the plan) and probes it for each outer row, or if the outer column is indexed it can flip the order and search the outer table by the inner values.

With the sample data the plan shows a scan of the covering index on orders, then a rowid search on customers. It does not re-run the inner query per row, because an IN subquery that is not correlated is evaluated once. Cost: O(M) to build the list plus O(N) cheap probes.

A JOIN wins when you need columns from the other table, not just a yes or no check. IN and EXISTS only filter and cannot return inner columns.

If the inner side can match many rows, a JOIN multiplies the outer row (3 orders for one customer give 3 rows), so you need DISTINCT or GROUP BY, which then costs extra. For a pure existence test EXISTS stops at the first match, so it avoids that duplication. Use JOIN when you want the data, EXISTS when you want only the test.

code.title: Subquery vs CTE for the same report
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE sales(region TEXT, rep TEXT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('N','a',100),('N','b',300),('S','c',200),('S','d',400),('S','e',600);
""")
# Subquery version: nested inside-out
sub = """SELECT region, total FROM
           (SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region)
         WHERE total > 500"""
# CTE version: named step, read top to bottom
cte = """WITH per_region AS (
           SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region)
         SELECT region, total FROM per_region WHERE total > 500"""
print("subquery:", db.execute(sub).fetchall())
print("cte     :", db.execute(cte).fetchall())
# A CTE can be reused several times in one statement
reuse = """WITH per_region AS (SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region)
           SELECT region, total, total * 100.0 / (SELECT SUM(total) FROM per_region) AS pct
           FROM per_region ORDER BY region"""
print("share of grand total:", db.execute(reuse).fetchall())

followUps:
Force MATERIALIZED when the CTE is expensive and referenced several times, or when you want it computed once as a fence against the optimizer pushing filters into it.

PostgreSQL 12+ inlines a CTE that is referenced once and not recursive, but WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...) computes it once and stores it. Example: a 10-second aggregate used by three later steps; materializing makes it 10 seconds total instead of 30. The downside is that the stored result has no statistics or indexes and filters cannot be pushed in.

A CTE lives for one statement, a temp table for one session, a view is a saved query that is re-expanded every time it is used.

  • CTE: readability, recursion, no storage.
  • Temp table: stored once, can be indexed and have statistics, good when reused across many statements or when the result is large.
  • View: reusable by everyone and hides logic, but it is only a name for the query, so nothing is cached.

Pick a temp table when an intermediate result is reused and needs an index.

code.title: Recursive CTE working table, step by step
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# Count 1..5 with a recursive CTE; I replay the same steps in Python to show the working table
print("SQL:", db.execute("""WITH RECURSIVE n(x) AS (
    SELECT 1                          -- anchor member
    UNION ALL
    SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5   -- recursive member sees only last round's rows
) SELECT x FROM n""").fetchall())

result, working = [], [1]             # step 1: anchor rows
round_no = 0
while working:                        # step 4: stop at a fixpoint (empty round)
    result += working                 # step 3: append to the result
    print("round", round_no, "working table:", working)
    # step 2: run the recursive member against the working table only
    working = [x + 1 for x in working if x < 5]
    round_no += 1
print("result:", result)

followUps:
Because aggregates need to see the whole input, and the recursive member only sees the small working table of the last round, so the result would be wrong and the engines forbid it.

Example: SUM(x) in the recursive member would add up only the latest round, not all earlier rows, and the next round would depend on a half-finished total. SQL Server and PostgreSQL reject aggregates, GROUP BY, DISTINCT and window functions there. Aggregate in the final SELECT after the recursion finishes instead.

Build a path (sort key) in each row and order by it; ordering by depth alone gives breadth-first order.

-- recursive member
SELECT e.id, t.path || ',' || printf('%03d', e.id)
FROM employees e JOIN team t ON e.manager_id = t.id
-- final query
ORDER BY path;

Zero-padding the ids keeps 10 after 9 as text. Sorting by path puts each child directly under its parent. PostgreSQL also has SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord (14+).

code.title: All direct and indirect reports
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INT);
CREATE INDEX ix_mgr ON employees(manager_id);
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Ravi',NULL),(2,'Sam',1),(3,'Tia',1),(4,'Uma',2),(5,'Vik',4),(6,'Wen',3),(7,'Xan',NULL);
""")
q = """
WITH RECURSIVE team(id, name, lvl) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE name = 'Ravi'   -- anchor: the manager
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, t.lvl + 1                           -- people reporting to last round
  FROM employees e JOIN team t ON e.manager_id = t.id
)
SELECT name, lvl FROM team WHERE lvl > 0 ORDER BY lvl, name"""
print("employees:", db.execute("SELECT id, name, manager_id FROM employees").fetchall())
for name, lvl in db.execute(q):
    print("  " * lvl + name, "(level %d)" % lvl)

followUps:
Make the anchor the employee and walk up by swapping the join direction: find the manager of the row found last round.

WITH RECURSIVE up(id, manager_id) AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id FROM employees WHERE name = 'Vik'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id
  FROM employees e JOIN up ON e.id = up.manager_id)
SELECT * FROM up;

For Vik this returns Vik, Uma, Sam, Ravi. Each round touches one row, so it is O(depth) with a primary key lookup.

Run the recursion once with the manager id carried through, then count descendants per root, or count with a closure table.

WITH RECURSIVE t(root, id) AS (
  SELECT id, id FROM employees
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.root, e.id FROM employees e JOIN t ON e.manager_id = t.id)
SELECT root, COUNT(*) - 1 AS team_size FROM t GROUP BY root;

The anchor starts a walk from every employee. Output size is the sum of all subtree sizes, up to O(N x depth).

code.title: Cycle-safe recursive walk with a path string
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE edge(a INT, b INT);
INSERT INTO edge VALUES (1,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,4);   -- 1->2->3->1 is a cycle
""")
q = """
WITH RECURSIVE walk(node, path, depth) AS (
  SELECT 1, ',1,', 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.b, w.path || e.b || ',', w.depth + 1
  FROM walk w JOIN edge e ON e.a = w.node
  WHERE instr(w.path, ',' || e.b || ',') = 0   -- refuse an already visited node
    AND w.depth < 10                           -- depth cap as a backstop
)
SELECT path FROM walk ORDER BY depth"""
print("edges:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM edge").fetchall())
for (p,) in db.execute(q):
    print("path", p)
# Reachability only: UNION de-duplicates nodes, so it stops by itself
r = db.execute("""WITH RECURSIVE r(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION
      SELECT b FROM r JOIN edge ON a = n) SELECT n FROM r ORDER BY n""").fetchall()
print("reachable from 1:", [x[0] for x in r])

followUps:
Because ids can be substrings of each other: without delimiters, id 1 is found inside path '12' or '21' and you wrongly think 1 was visited.

With a path like ,1,2,12, searching for ,1, only matches a whole id. Searching plain 1 would match inside 12, so node 1 would be refused even though it was never seen. Wrap the path with a comma at both ends and search for ',' || id || ','.

It can be exponential, because the number of simple paths in a graph can grow with the factorial or exponential of the node count.

A fully connected graph of n nodes has about e x (n-1)! simple paths from one start; for n = 10 that is already about a million. The cycle check only stops infinite loops, it does not reduce the output. If you only need reachability or shortest distance use UNION on node ids, which is O(V + E).

code.title: Calendar of dates with zero-revenue days
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_date TEXT, status TEXT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,'2024-07-01','paid',100),(2,'2024-07-01','paid',50),
 (3,'2024-07-03','cancelled',80),(4,'2024-07-03','paid',20),(5,'2024-07-06','paid',70);
""")
q = """
WITH RECURSIVE days(d) AS (
  SELECT '2024-07-01'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(d, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE d < '2024-07-07'   -- calendar rows
)
SELECT d, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS revenue      -- missing days become 0
FROM days
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = d AND o.status <> 'cancelled'  -- filter in ON
GROUP BY d ORDER BY d"""
for d, rev in db.execute(q):
    print(d, rev)

followUps:
Because the WHERE on the right table runs after the join and removes the rows where the right side is NULL, so the empty days vanish and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an inner join.

For 2024-07-02 there is no order, so o.status is NULL, and NULL <> 'cancelled' is UNKNOWN, so the row is dropped. Put the condition in ON and the day stays with revenue 0. A filter on the left (calendar) table is safe in WHERE.

Step the recursion by month instead of by day, and join on the month of the fact date.

WITH RECURSIVE m(d) AS (
  SELECT '2024-01-01'
  UNION ALL SELECT date(d, '+1 month') FROM m WHERE d < '2024-12-01')
SELECT m.d, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0)
FROM m LEFT JOIN orders o ON strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) = strftime('%Y-%m', m.d)
GROUP BY m.d;

Result: 12 rows, one per month, zero where nothing sold.

code.title: Second highest salary with ties and empty case
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INT);
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'A',90),(2,'B',90),(3,'C',80),(4,'D',70);
""")
print("salaries:", db.execute("SELECT salary FROM employees").fetchall())
n = 2
q = {
 "MAX < MAX": "SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)",
 "DISTINCT+OFFSET": "SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET %d)" % (n - 1),
 "DENSE_RANK": """SELECT salary FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) r
                  FROM employees) WHERE r = %d LIMIT 1""" % n,
 "buggy OFFSET (no DISTINCT)": "SELECT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET %d" % (n - 1),
}
for k, v in q.items():
    print(k, "->", db.execute(v).fetchall())   # buggy one returns 90, the top value
# Empty case: 10th highest gives NULL (None) with the scalar wrapper
print("10th:", db.execute("SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 9)").fetchall())

followUps:
Compute the rank inside each department with DENSE_RANK and keep rank N, using PARTITION BY dept.

SELECT dept, salary FROM (
  SELECT dept, salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) r
  FROM employees) WHERE r = 2;

A department with only one distinct salary simply has no row, so to show NULL join the result back to the department table. Cost is one sort per partition, O(N log N).

RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK does not, so for 'Nth highest salary' you want DENSE_RANK.

With salaries 90, 90, 80, 70: RANK gives 1, 1, 3, 4 and DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2, 3. The second highest salary is 80. RANK() = 2 returns nothing because no row has rank 2, while DENSE_RANK() = 2 correctly returns 80.

code.title: Window function vs correlated subquery
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE emp(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept INT, salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Asha',1,50),(2,'Ben',1,70),(3,'Cy',2,40),(4,'Di',2,90),(5,'Eli',2,50);
""")
# Correlated: logically re-runs the inner query for every outer row
corr = """SELECT name, salary, (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept) AS avg_dept
          FROM emp e ORDER BY id"""
# Window: one pass, partitioned by dept
win = "SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS avg_dept FROM emp ORDER BY id"
print("correlated:", db.execute(corr).fetchall())
print("window    :", db.execute(win).fetchall())
# Window results cannot be filtered in the same SELECT: wrap in a CTE
top = """WITH r AS (SELECT name, dept, salary,
                    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) rn FROM emp)
         SELECT dept, name FROM r WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY dept"""
print("top earner per dept:", db.execute(top).fetchall())

followUps:
Using a correlated subquery for the top earner:

SELECT name, dept FROM emp e
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept);

Using a window function, which reads emp once:

SELECT name, dept FROM (
  SELECT name, dept, ROW_NUMBER() OVER
    (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) rn FROM emp) WHERE rn = 1;

With ties on top, the subquery returns all tied people while ROW_NUMBER returns one (use RANK to keep ties).

No, not in the recursive member; engines forbid window functions there for the same reason as aggregates, since the member sees only the last round.

You can use window functions in the anchor and in the final SELECT over the finished result. For example, compute ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY lvl ORDER BY name) after the recursion ends. To number rows per round inside the recursion carry a counter in a column instead.

code.title: The COUNT bug when unnesting a subquery
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE cust(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE ord(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, cust_id INT);
INSERT INTO cust VALUES (1,'Ana'),(2,'Bo'),(3,'Cat');
INSERT INTO ord VALUES (10,1),(11,1),(12,3);   -- Bo has no orders
""")
orig = "SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ord o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id) AS n FROM cust c ORDER BY id"
# Naive unnesting (the COUNT bug): inner join with a grouped table drops Bo
buggy = """SELECT c.name, g.n FROM cust c
           JOIN (SELECT cust_id, COUNT(*) n FROM ord GROUP BY cust_id) g ON g.cust_id = c.id
           ORDER BY c.id"""
# Correct unnesting: LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE(count, 0)
fixed = """SELECT c.name, COALESCE(g.n, 0) FROM cust c
           LEFT JOIN (SELECT cust_id, COUNT(*) n FROM ord GROUP BY cust_id) g ON g.cust_id = c.id
           ORDER BY c.id"""
print("correlated :", db.execute(orig).fetchall())
print("buggy join :", db.execute(buggy).fetchall())
print("fixed join :", db.execute(fixed).fetchall())

followUps:
Engines that memoize (cache) correlated subquery results per distinct outer key include PostgreSQL (Memoize node, version 14+), MySQL 8 with its subquery materialization, and Oracle with scalar subquery caching.

If 1,000,000 rows have only 50 distinct dept values, memoizing runs the inner query 50 times instead of 1,000,000. This only helps when the correlation key repeats a lot. SQLite does not cache it, so it runs the inner query for every row unless indexed.

LATERAL (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8) or CROSS APPLY (SQL Server) lets a subquery in FROM refer to columns of tables that appear before it, so it can return several rows and columns per outer row.

SELECT c.name, t.id FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT id FROM orders o
  WHERE o.cust_id = c.id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3) t;

This gives the last 3 orders per customer, which a scalar subquery cannot. SQLite has no LATERAL.

code.title: Category tree: recursive CTE vs closure table
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE cat(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, parent_id INT);
INSERT INTO cat VALUES (1,'Root',NULL),(2,'Electronics',1),(3,'Phones',2),(4,'Laptops',2),(5,'Gaming',4);
-- Closure table: one row per (ancestor, descendant) pair, built from the adjacency list
CREATE TABLE closure(anc INT, des INT, depth INT);
INSERT INTO closure
WITH RECURSIVE c(anc, des, depth) AS (
  SELECT id, id, 0 FROM cat
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.anc, k.id, c.depth + 1 FROM c JOIN cat k ON k.parent_id = c.des)
SELECT * FROM c;
""")
# Adjacency list: subtree needs a recursive CTE
rec = """WITH RECURSIVE s(id) AS (SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT k.id FROM cat k JOIN s ON k.parent_id = s.id)
         SELECT name FROM cat WHERE id IN s ORDER BY id"""
# Closure table: subtree is one indexed join
clo = "SELECT k.name FROM closure c JOIN cat k ON k.id = c.des WHERE c.anc = 2 ORDER BY k.id"
# Ancestors (breadcrumb) of 'Gaming'
bread = "SELECT k.name FROM closure c JOIN cat k ON k.id = c.anc WHERE c.des = 5 ORDER BY c.depth DESC"
print("subtree (recursive):", [r[0] for r in db.execute(rec)])
print("subtree (closure)  :", [r[0] for r in db.execute(clo)])
print("breadcrumb of Gaming:", [r[0] for r in db.execute(bread)])
print("closure rows:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM closure").fetchone()[0])

followUps:
Adjacency list: update one parent_id. Materialized path: rewrite the path prefix of every descendant. Nested sets: renumber lft and rgt for a large part of the tree. Closure table: delete the old ancestor links and insert new ones.

Moving a node with 1,000 descendants costs 1 row update in the adjacency list, 1,001 in a path model, up to the whole table in nested sets, and roughly 1,001 x depth in the closure table. Do it in one transaction.

Before moving or inserting a node, check that the new parent is not the node itself or one of its descendants.

With a closure table: refuse if EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM closure WHERE anc = :node AND des = :new_parent). With an adjacency list, run an upward recursive CTE from the new parent and reject if it reaches the node. Add a CHECK that id <> parent_id, and do the check and the write in one transaction so two moves cannot race.

code.title: Replace SELECT-list subqueries with one grouped join

followUps:
Because the join of ord with item repeats each order once per item line, so COUNT(*) would count item rows, not orders.

Order 10 has two items (qty 2 and 1). After the join order 10 appears twice, so COUNT(*) gives 3 for Ana's two orders, while COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) gives 2. SUM(i.qty) is still correct since each item row is counted once. Better still, aggregate items per order before joining.

A materialized CTE is computed in full with no indexes or statistics, so a join to it can pick a poor plan and scan it for every outer row.

If the CTE returns 1 million rows and you only need 10 customers, the filter cannot be pushed inside, so you pay for 1 million rows. Fix it by filtering inside the CTE, by letting the engine inline it (NOT MATERIALIZED in PostgreSQL), or by creating a temp table with an index.

code.title: Relational division with double NOT EXISTS

followUps:
Exact division means the customer bought precisely the products in the category and nothing outside it; add a second condition that no purchased product is outside the set.

-- plus: bought nothing outside the category
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND p.category <> 'Electronics')

Or compare counts: distinct bought equals category size and equals total distinct bought.

The counting version (GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT) = category size) usually scales better, since it is one pass with a hash aggregate, roughly O(rows).

The double NOT EXISTS is a nested loop in the worst case: for each customer, for each product, an index probe, which is O(C x P x log). With indexes on (customer_id) and (product_id) both are fine for small categories. Test both with EXPLAIN on real data, and remember the counting version needs DISTINCT to ignore repeat purchases.
